title: switch, case, default and fall-through
learningObjectives: Write switch statements using an integer or enumeration controlling expression.
Use case labels and an optional default label correctly.
Explain fall-through and use break when a case should stop.
Recognize that case labels must be integer constant expressions and cannot duplicate values.
Choose between switch and if/else based on the decision being represented.

understand.concept: A switch statement selects a matching case label based on an integer or enumeration controlling expression. Case labels are integer constant expressions and must be unique within the switch. Execution continues from the selected label until a break, return or the end of the switch, so accidental fall-through is a common defect. The optional default label handles values with no matching case.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding switch, case, default and fall-through helps you reason about program behaviour instead of memorizing syntax. It is useful in exams, debugging and building reliable C applications.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a tool with a precise contract: it has valid inputs, defined operations and observable results.
understand.analogyLimit: An analogy is only an aid; the C standard and the relevant function specifications determine actual behaviour.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Basic switch structure

A switch evaluates its controlling expression and transfers control to the matching case label. The controlling expression must have an integer type after the applicable promotions, or be an enumeration type.

## 2. Case labels

Each case label uses an integer constant expression. Case values must be distinct within the same switch. They are not general run-time conditions, so a variable cannot be used as a case value.

## 3. break and fall-through

A break exits the nearest enclosing switch. Without break, execution continues into the next case body. This is called fall-through. It can be intentional, but should be clearly documented; otherwise add break or another control transfer.

## 4. default

The optional default label runs when no case value matches. It is useful for invalid or unexpected input. It can appear anywhere in the switch, though placing it last is a common style.

## 5. Choose the right tool

Use switch for a selection among discrete constant values. Use if/else for ranges, compound conditions or comparisons that are not simple case labels.

questions.prompt: What type can control a C switch statement?
options: An integer or enumeration type after applicable promotions
questions.answer: An integer or enumeration type after applicable promotions
questions.explanation: The switch controlling expression must have an integer or enumeration type.

questions.prompt: What happens if a case has no break or other control transfer?
options: Execution can continue into the following case body
The switch ends automatically at the next label
questions.answer: Execution can continue into the following case body

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of default?
options: Handle values that match no case label
questions.answer: Handle values that match no case label
questions.explanation: The default label is selected when no case value matches.

questions.prompt: Can a case label use a run-time variable?
options: No; it must be an integer constant expression
Only if the variable is global
questions.answer: No; it must be an integer constant expression
questions.explanation: Case labels are compile-time integer constant expressions.

questions.prompt: When is if/else generally more appropriate than switch?
options: When testing ranges or compound conditions
When selecting among fixed integer labels only
questions.answer: When testing ranges or compound conditions
questions.explanation: switch labels represent discrete constant values, not arbitrary predicates.
